records.text: One of the oldest patterns in chess: the fork. A single piece attacks several targets, and the defender can rescue only one of them.
The fork is an old weapon, and it serves either side. This move lets the other side set one up, with a single piece reaching for several targets at once.
A fork was on offer in another move: one piece, several targets, and only one of them able to escape. This move leaves that pattern unused.
Here is the pin to the king, a pattern worth knowing by heart. The pinned piece must stay on its line, because stepping aside would expose its own king.
A pin binds a piece to the king behind it. This move lets the other side apply one, and the pinned piece would then be held on its line.
A different move would have pinned one of their pieces to its king. Held like that, it cannot leave the line without exposing the king. The pattern goes unused here.
The skewer is the pin turned around. The valuable piece stands in front; when it steps aside, the piece behind it is laid open.
Beware the skewer, the pin's reversed cousin. This gives the other side one: the front piece may have to move and leave the piece behind it exposed.
A stronger move held a skewer. Strike the front piece, and once it steps away, the piece standing behind it is exposed. The pattern was there to use.
An old principle: to win what is guarded, remove the guard. This move captures a defender, so study what that defender was protecting.
What is guarded is only as safe as its guard. This lets the other side capture a defender, and whatever it protected could then stand without cover.
Another move could have removed a defender by capture, leaving whatever it guarded without protection. A classic method, and it was available.
The back-rank mate is among the most reliable patterns there is. The king's own pieces wall it in, and an attacker on the last rank finishes the work.
Mark this pattern well: the back-rank mate. This move gives the other side a route to it, with the king hemmed in by its own pieces.
A back-rank mate was within reach, the king boxed in by its own guards. This move lets that well-known finish slip away.
Every pawn carries the possibility of a queen. The idea here is promotion, so follow the pawn's road to the last rank.
A pawn near the last rank deserves constant attention. This opens a path to promotion for the other side; trace the pawn that could make the journey.
A stronger move opened the road to promotion for a pawn. This move leaves that pawn short of the last rank, and the chance passes.
The discovered attack is a fine old device. One piece steps out of the way, and the piece behind it strikes along the line it uncovers.
A piece standing in front of another can hide a threat. This hands the other side a discovered attack, where the front piece steps away and the piece behind it strikes.
Another move held a discovered attack. The front piece would step aside, and the line behind it would open to a threat. The device stayed unused.
Two threats at once is a principle older than any opening. A single reply rarely answers both, and this move makes the double attack.
A position that allows two threats at once is hard to defend. This move gives the other side a double attack; find both threats before choosing an answer.
A stronger move created two threats at once. This one passes over that double attack, and with it the hardest kind of problem for a defender.
Deflection is an old lesson: a defender cannot guard a post it has been lured away from. This move draws one off, and its duty is left unattended.
A defender with an important duty can be lured away. This move gives the other side that deflection, so mark what the defender is holding now.
Another move could have lured a defender away from its duty. The deflection stayed on the shelf; study what the defender had to hold.
The simplest principle of all still applies, and an unguarded piece falls to the first attacker. This move captures one. Before any combination, count the loose pieces.
Another move could have collected an unguarded piece. This one walks past it. Loose pieces should be counted before anything more elaborate.
Pieces without a guard invite capture. This move leaves one for the other side to take; look for the piece that has lost its protection.
A defender has a duty before it has a destination. This move takes away a piece's only real defender, and the other side can now capture what it guarded.
Every move asks a question, and the opponent's last one created a threat. This move leaves it unanswered, so a piece can now be captured.
An exchange is judged after the recapture, not before. This capture invites the other side to take back a more valuable piece.
Development is the first principle of the opening. This brings a minor piece off its home square; note where it now stands.
Another move would have developed a minor piece from its home square. The opening rewards each piece that joins the game.
Rooks belong on open files; that is one of the steadiest rules we have. This leaves a rook on a file with no pawns of either color.
Another move would have placed a rook on an open file, clear of pawns of both colors. Rooks are at their best on such roads.
A semi-open file is the next best thing for a rook. This rook has no friendly pawns on its file, though at least one enemy pawn remains.
Another move would have given a rook a semi-open file, free of its own pawns, with an enemy pawn still standing there.
A passed pawn is a lasting asset. This leaves one, with its own file and both neighboring files free of enemy pawns ahead of it.
Another move would have produced a passed pawn, with no enemy pawn ahead of it on its file or the files beside it.
Passed pawns must be pushed, as the old saying has it. This one was already passed, and the move carries it further forward.
Another move would have pushed the passed pawn onward. Compare where it could have stood with where it stays.
An isolated pawn has no neighbor to lean on. This move leaves one, with no friendly pawn on either adjacent file.
Another move would have left an isolated pawn, without a friendly pawn on either neighboring file.
A guarded piece is a calm piece. This move gives a piece the defender it lacked.
Another move would have given an unguarded piece a defender, so it would no longer stand alone.
After this move, a piece stands with no defender. An undefended piece is a weakness, but not yet proof that it can be won.
Another move would have left a piece without a guard. By itself, that would not prove the piece could be won.
A king with an escape square is harder to trap. This move opens a legal flight square that was not there before; compare the positions to see what cleared it.
Another move would have opened a new legal square for the king. Compare the two positions to find what would have cleared the way.
Castling serves two old purposes at once. The king steps toward shelter, and the rook comes toward the center.
The other choice was to castle, moving king and rook together in a single turn.
The two bishops together cover every square color, and that partnership is often valued. This capture ends the bishop pair for the side that loses the bishop.
Another move would have captured a bishop and dissolved the opposing bishop pair.
Doubled pawns are a familiar structural weakness. This leaves two pawns of the same color on a single file.
Another move would have left doubled pawns, two of one color stacked on the same file.
The king's safety outranks every other lesson. Here the move permits a forced checkmate; trace the attack to the point where the defense gives way.
A forced checkmate was waiting, and this move lets it go. Return to the position; the finish is worth finding and remembering.
A sacrifice is tested by its acceptance. Here the offered material can be taken, and the idea still holds in the line that was checked.
Some positions offer a single narrow path. Of the moves examined, only this one kept the position playable, and every other one was losing.
Of the moves examined, only this one kept the advantage. Every other choice was losing, so this move carried the whole position.
Look first at what the reply can take. The other side has a capture available at once.
A check must be answered before all else. The strongest reply gives check, so the king's safety comes first.
The engine favors another move here. Set the two side by side on the board and compare what the replies allow.
By the engine's measure, this falls short of the best option. The reply is where the difference becomes visible.
Among the moves the engine examined, this is a strong choice. Well judged.
Sound, and worth respecting. The engine has another preference, yet this keeps most of what the position offered.
The human-move model rates this a natural choice, and the engine finds a stronger one. The most tempting move is not always the soundest; that lesson is worth keeping.
The human-move model rates this an unusual choice, and the engine finds it strong. A rare move can still be a sound one.
The engine found one move that kept the position playable, and the human-move model rates it hard to find. Difficult defenses are learned by studying them.
The human-move model and the searched alternatives both point to a hard move to find. Store the idea; it will serve again in similar positions.
This move kept the position playable, and the human-move model and the searched alternatives mark it as a hard defense to find. A resource well found.
The human-move model rates this a natural choice, and it is also the engine's best move. Here intuition and calculation reach the same conclusion.
The human-move model rates this a natural choice, and the engine finds it strong, though it prefers another move.
The recorded clock shows very little time remained before this move. Time is part of the position too.
The recorded clock shows this move came quickly, with time still in reserve.
The recorded clock shows a long deliberation over this move.
This move stands in a recognized opening line, a road many games have traveled before.
Here the game steps past the last move our opening book recognizes. From this point, the position must be read on its own terms.
The earlier setback is answered here, and the position is playable once more. A setback need not be the end of the lesson.
After the earlier setback, the position is playable again, and errors by the other side helped make that recovery possible.
The opponent's last move offered an opportunity, and this move takes it. Recognizing a gift is a skill of its own.
An opportunity came with the opponent's last move, and this move does not take it. Go back one move and look for the stronger answer.
This issue has already appeared earlier in the reviewed game. When a pattern repeats, set the examples side by side and find the common warning sign.
A piece left unguarded earlier is defended once more. Compare the two positions to see how its protection returned.
Small concessions accumulate quietly. This move is one of several that have worn the position down together, so study the sequence rather than this move alone.
The advantage was carried all the way to the recorded win. Conversion is a craft of its own; follow that stretch to see how it was done.
Your other saved games show this same issue. A pattern seen in several games is a pattern worth studying across all of them.
Checkmate. The king has no legal escape, and the attack is complete. A finish worth remembering.
Checkmate. Every legal square is closed to the king, and the lesson lies earlier, in the moment the defense could still have held.
A drawn game. The result is settled, though the decisions along the way still have much to teach.
Study the position before you act, and only then decide on a move.
That attempt does not survive the reply. Return to the position and look for the pattern it contains.
The attempt brought back no result. Come back to the move and try it once more.
The saved engine analysis finds a forced checkmate here for the side that made this move.
In the saved engine analysis, this move gives the other side a forced checkmate.
By the end of the saved line, the side that made this move has gained material compared with the starting position.
By the end of the saved line, the side that made this move has lost material compared with the starting position.
This move is accepted for the exercise, though the moves shown offer no clear tactical explanation, and I will not invent one.
The exercise does not accept this move, and the moves shown give no clear tactical reason. Study the position again with fresh eyes.
This move matches one of the saved answers. In this exercise, the saved answers are the measure.
This move is not among the saved answers for the exercise. A different legal move is not, on that account alone, bad chess.
Study the move with care, then go on to the next position.
Good. Keep its reason alongside it; the reason is what returns when the pattern does.
Your practice is saved, and the review schedule stands as it was.
Solved. This recall remains marked for relearning, all the same.
This is the starting position, before any of the moves we will study.
Here is the following move. Note what it changes.
Check. The king is attacked, and that must be answered first.
This move brings the king out of check.
The pawn completes its journey to the last rank and promotes.
The pawn promotes on the last rank, and the new piece gives check.
The pawn promotes on the last rank, and the result is checkmate. No legal escape remains for that king.
The pawn promotes on the last rank, and the move also lifts the check on its own king.
A capture: one piece leaves the board.
This captures a piece, and the same move gives check.
This capture is also checkmate. The king has no legal square to escape to.
This capture also brings the king out of check.
The pawn captures onto the last rank and promotes in a single stroke.
The pawn captures onto the last rank and promotes, and the new piece gives check.
The pawn captures onto the last rank and promotes, and that is checkmate, with every legal square closed to the king.
The pawn captures onto the last rank and promotes, and in doing so it frees its own king from check.
The king castles, the rook crosses over, and the move gives check as well.
The king castles, the rook crosses over, and the result is checkmate. No legal flight remains for the opposing king.
The fork, demonstrated: one piece attacks several targets and then takes one of them. The example also ends with a net material gain.
This piece is pinned to its king, so it cannot make the marked capture. Leaving the line would expose the king, and that is not permitted.
The attacked piece is pinned to its king, which limits its escape. Any move it makes must still keep the king covered.
The defenders are pinned to their king, so they cannot recapture on that square. That is why the capture works, and the line shown ends with a material gain.
Follow the pinned piece. It cannot leave its line without exposing the king, and as these moves unfold, it is captured.
The front piece steps off the line, and the piece behind it is captured along that same line. The skewer, completed.
The king must step out of check and off the line. The same attacker then collects whatever stood behind the king.
First the lone defender is captured, then the piece it was guarding. Mark how the first capture makes the second possible.
The defender is lured from its post, and what it was guarding falls in its absence.
The blocker moves aside, and a line opens behind it. The piece on that line makes the capture.
A piece steps off the line, and the one behind it delivers check: the discovered check.
Double check: two pieces attack the king together, and only a king move can answer both.
The moving piece makes one attack and uncovers a second along the line it leaves. In the example, that second piece completes the capture.
Follow the pawn to its promotion. The example also records a net material gain for that side.
An undefended piece is taken here. The example shows a net material gain for the side that captures.
The opponent's previous move released the attacking piece from a relative pin. The target was left where it stood, and in the line shown it is captured.
The marked reply is a legal move for the other side. Play it on the board and study what follows.
Before you move, survey your own pieces for any that could be taken without a useful recapture.
Before settling on a quiet move, survey the board for loose enemy pieces.
Examine the forcing moves for a single piece that can strike two valuable targets at once.
A pinned piece shields something behind it. Before moving one, see whether that is your king or a piece of greater value.
The first target is not always the whole story. Follow the line past it, to any valuable piece standing further back.
A defender's value includes everything it protects. Before exchanging one, see what depends on it.
When a blocking piece moves, study the lines it opens behind it.
Search for one move that creates two threats, and remember that checks and opened lines count among them.
Before a back-rank defender moves, make certain your king still has an escape square.
Count the steps a pawn needs to promote, and study the pawn advances that force a reply.
Before a defender moves, list every piece that relies on its protection.
Weigh what you capture against what the recapture takes back. The exchange is judged as a whole.
See whether a forcing exchange can lure a defender away from a second duty.
In this exercise, the saved answers are the authority. A different legal move is not, on that account alone, poor chess.
These moves show how play could unfold against strong replies. Strong replies are not always forced ones.
Any material change here belongs only to the line shown, counted from its own starting position. The piece values behind that count are listed in the written explanation.
The saved line establishes no simple tactical reason, and no positional explanation has been inferred. Walk through it move by move and weigh the replies on your own.
The answer policy saved for this exercise governs the explanation. The written notes record its setting.
These are the moves of the opening line under your study.
Correct. That move is in your chosen study material.
Play a move drawn from your selected study lines.
A move from any of your selected opening lines will be accepted.
Bring to mind a move from the material you chose to study.
Your selected opening lines do not include that move. Try a different one.
That move lies outside your selected opening lines, so try once more. Because the study has changed, this saved attempt leaves its review schedule untouched.
That move lies outside your selected opening lines, so try once more. This position is retired, and its review schedule stays as it is.
When you practice in mixed Due, this line supplies acceptable moves. Dedicated practice asks for this line and no other.
Your scheduled recalls will ask you to play your selected side's moves. Where your active studies share a position, they share a single card.
Please reload the saved session before you play another move.
The board now plays through the verified line.
Your attempt is saved as revealed. The solution can be replayed below whenever you wish.
After a retry, you found the full solution. Your record keeps both the earlier miss and the finish.
The full solution, without a single wrong move. Excellent work.
The puzzle is not solved by that move. Every correct move you made before it is still saved.
Correct, that move fits the puzzle. Now look for the move that follows.
Calculate patiently before you move. The pattern is in the position.
The engine has not given me enough to explain this position, and I will not guess at it.
Your review rests here for now. Resume it below, or move a piece to explore on your own.
Pick any move to study, or move a piece yourself to test another idea.
This move is in the book. The position has its place in the opening literature.
The opening books record this move. We stand on charted ground.
A recognized opening move, already set down in the opening literature.
The opening literature still records this move.
The book continues; its pages have not run out yet.
The reply, too, is written in the book.
Charted ground still; the opening record goes on.
Another move with an entry in the opening literature.
The book still keeps an entry for this one.
Still within recorded opening theory.
The book holds this move as well. Its place in the book is a matter of record, not a verdict on its quality.

The human-move model rates this a natural choice, and yet it allows a forced checkmate. The most inviting move can be the one that opens the gate; trace the attack to the point where the defense gives way.

A forced checkmate was waiting, and this move lets it go. The human-move model finds the move natural, which is exactly why the lesson matters: when a finish is on the board, look for it before anything else.
By the human-move model's estimate this is a natural move, yet the other side can capture at once. Before admiring a move, look at what the very next reply can take.
The human-move model counts this move natural, and the engine still finds a stronger one. The appealing choice and the sound one part ways here, and the reply marks the spot.
Natural, in the human-move model's view, but it hands the other side a fork. One of their pieces can reach several targets at once, so find that piece before anything else.
To the human-move model this looks natural, and it opens a skewer for the other side. When the front piece is driven off its line, the piece behind it may be exposed.
A narrow path, and you walked it. Of the moves examined, only this one kept the position playable, and the human-move model rates it a hard defense to find. Well found.

The position stayed playable through this move alone; each of the other moves examined was losing. It heads the engine's list, and the human-move model rates it hard to find. Resources like this are worth committing to memory.
Of every move examined, this alone kept the advantage, and the rest were losing. The human-move model rates it a hard resource to find, which makes finding it all the more creditable.

The advantage rested on this one move; each of the other moves examined was losing. The engine places it first, while the human-move model and the searched alternatives mark it as a difficult find. Hold on to the reason as well as the move.
Here is the fork, one piece reaching several targets at once. The human-move model would not expect it, yet the engine holds it strong. Patterns do not care whether a move looks ordinary.
A fork, and a well-hidden one: a single piece against several targets. Best by the engine's reckoning, and hard to find by the human-move model's. That is the kind of pattern that rewards study.
This pins a piece to its king, and the pinned piece cannot leave its line without exposing the king behind it. The human-move model rates it an uncommon choice, and the engine rates it strong.
Here the pin to the king holds a piece fast; it must stay on its line or expose its king. It is the engine's first choice, and one the human-move model counts among the hard finds.

A defender's first duty is the piece it guards. This move, natural by the human-move model's estimate, takes away a piece's only real defender, and the other side can now capture what was left behind.

This move takes away a piece's only real defender, so the other side can capture what it guarded. Only one move examined kept the position playable, and the human-move model rates it a hard defense to find.
Begin with what the opponent's last move changed: it created a threat. This move, natural to the human-move model, leaves the threat unanswered, and a piece can now be captured.
The opponent's last move created a threat, and this move leaves it standing, so a piece can be captured. A single move examined held, and the human-move model marks it as a difficult defense.
The capture feels natural, and the human-move model agrees, but the recapture takes a more valuable piece. Judge an exchange only when every recapture has been counted.

After this capture, the other side recaptures a piece of greater value. The search found one defense that held, and the human-move model counts it among the hard ones to see. Weigh that resource against the whole exchange.
One piece reaching several targets: the fork. The human-move model expects this move, and the engine places it first. When the obvious move carries the pattern, play it with confidence.
There is a fork in this move, one piece aiming at several targets. The human-move model counts it natural, and the engine holds it strong, though another move heads its list.
This lets the other side set up a fork, with one piece reaching several targets. One move alone held the position, and by the human-move model's estimate it was not easy to find.
Another move held a fork, one piece against several targets. This move is natural to the human-move model, and the fork is left unplayed. The tempting move is not always the one with the pattern.
The only move that kept the position playable contained a fork, one piece reaching several targets. It went unplayed, and the human-move model rates that defense hard to find.

The pinned piece is held on its line, because stepping away would expose its king. By the human-move model's reckoning it is a natural move, and the engine can find nothing better. Instinct and principle agree.
This pins a piece to its king, so the piece cannot leave its line. Natural by the human-move model's estimate, and strong by the engine's, which keeps a different first choice.
The human-move model counts this natural, but it lets the other side pin a piece to its king. Once pinned, that piece is held on its line.
This gives the other side a pin to the king. The lone playable defense was a different move, and the human-move model rates it hard to spot.
A stronger move could have pinned a piece to its king, holding it on its line. This move is natural by the human-move model's estimate, and the pin goes unused.
The single playable move used a pin to the king, freezing a piece on its line. It was missed, and the human-move model rates it hard to find. Study it; pins return in many forms.

Drive the front piece off its line, and the piece behind it is exposed: the skewer. The engine rates it highest; the human-move model and the moves searched beside it say it was not easily found. Fine work.

Here is the skewer, the pin's reversed form. When the front piece moves, the piece behind it is laid open. An unexpected move, as the human-move model sees it, and a strong one, as the engine sees it.
The front piece moves, and the piece behind it is exposed along the same line. It is the move the human-move model expects, and the engine's first choice besides.
This move carries a skewer. Once the front piece steps aside, the piece behind it can be attacked. The human-move model expects it, and the engine approves it as strong while preferring another move.

This gives the other side a skewer, where the front piece may have to move and expose the one behind it. Just one examined move kept the game playable, a defense the human-move model rates as difficult.
A stronger move had a skewer, the front piece driven off to expose the piece behind. This move is natural to the human-move model, and the skewer stays unused.
The only playable move found carried a skewer: move the front piece off the line, and the one behind is exposed. It was missed, and the human-move model counts it among the hard finds.
Remove the guard, and what it guarded stands alone. This move captures the defender. The engine's best, and by the human-move model's estimate a difficult one to see.
An old method: capture the defender, and the piece it protected loses its cover. It lies off the human-move model's usual paths, yet the engine finds it strong.
The defender falls first, and what it covered is left unprotected. The human-move model counts it natural; the engine counts it best. The principle and the instinct point the same way.
This captures a defender, so the piece it covered loses its protection. The human-move model takes it for a natural move; the engine takes it for a strong one, though not its first choice.
The human-move model counts this a natural move, and it leaves a defender open to capture. Should that defender fall, whatever it guards may be left uncovered.
This exposes a defender to capture, and whatever it guards could then go unprotected. Only one move examined kept the position playable, and the human-move model rates it a hard defense to find.
Another move could have taken a defender off the board, along with the protection it gave. This move is natural to the human-move model, and the defender keeps its post.
The single playable move captured a defender and removed the protection it gave. It went unplayed, and the human-move model marks it as hard to find.
The back-rank pattern: the king's own pieces form the wall that traps it. The engine sets it above every other move, and the human-move model marks it as hard to find. A classic, well found.
The king is walled in by its own pieces, the classic picture of the back-rank mate. The human-move model marks it unusual; the engine marks it strong.

The pieces meant to shelter the king are the very ones that box it in. That is the back-rank idea. Intuition, as the human-move model measures it, and the engine's calculation arrive at the same move.
There is a back-rank mating idea here, the king hemmed in by its own pieces. It comes naturally, in the human-move model's view, and the engine rates it strong, though it would choose differently.
Promotion is the goal here, a pawn bound for the last rank. This is the engine's best move, and the human-move model and the searched alternatives agree it was hard to find.
A pawn sets out on the road toward the last rank and promotion. Unusual by the human-move model's measure, and strong by the engine's. Never underestimate a pawn on the march.
The idea is promotion, a pawn advancing toward the last rank. The human-move model sees a natural move here, and the engine sees its best. A pawn's journey, rightly begun.
Promotion is the idea, with a pawn pressing toward the last rank. The human-move model names it a natural choice; the engine names it strong and still ranks another move above it.
The human-move model finds this natural, but it gives one of the other side's pawns a path to promotion. Follow that pawn all the way to the last rank.
This gives the other side's pawn a road toward promotion. A single move examined held, and the human-move model marks it as a difficult defense.
Another move would have set a pawn on its way to promotion. This move is natural by the human-move model's estimate, and the pawn stays where it was.
The only playable move found sent a pawn toward promotion. It went unplayed, and the human-move model rates that resource hard to find.

One piece steps aside, and the piece behind it strikes along the open line. First on the engine's list, and well hidden by the human-move model's estimate. A discovered attack hides behind another piece; that is its nature.
One piece moves out of the way, and the piece behind it attacks; the discovered attack at work. The human-move model does not expect it, and the engine judges it strong all the same.
Move the front piece, and the one behind it begins to attack. Natural by the human-move model's estimate, and best by the engine's.
A blocker steps aside here and uncovers an attack from the piece behind it. To the human-move model this is natural, and to the engine it is strong, with a different move on top.
Natural, says the human-move model, but it allows a discovered attack. One of the other side's pieces could step off the line and let the piece behind it strike.
This allows a discovered attack, one piece stepping aside to reveal another. The search found one defense that held, and the human-move model counts it among the hard ones to see.
Another move held a discovered attack, with a front piece stepping aside so the one behind could strike. This move is natural to the human-move model, and the device stays unused.
The single playable move used a discovered attack, a piece stepping aside to open another's line. It was missed, and the human-move model rates it hard to find.
Two threats at once, and a reply can rarely meet both. The engine rates it best, and the human-move model rates it hard to see. Well calculated.
One move, two threats, and a single reply to face them. Rare in the human-move model's estimate, strong in the engine's.
Two threats with a single move. Here the human-move model's natural choice and the engine's best are one move. The principle and the instinct agree.
This double attack poses two threats, each demanding its own answer. The human-move model finds nothing surprising in it, and the engine finds it strong, while preferring another move.
The human-move model counts this natural, yet it gives the other side a double attack. Two threats would arrive together, and each would need its own answer.
This lets the other side make a double attack, two threats at the same moment. One move alone held the position, and by the human-move model's estimate it was not easy to find.
A different move would have made two threats at once. This one is natural by the human-move model's estimate, and the double attack is left unplayed.
The single playable move made two threats at once. It went unplayed, and the human-move model rates it a hard resource to spot.
Here a defender is coaxed away from the piece it guards. It heads the engine's list, and the human-move model rates it hard to find. Deflections reward a patient eye.
Lure a defender from its post, and its duty goes undone, which is the whole art of deflection. To the human-move model this is an unusual choice; to the engine, a strong one.
Draw the defender away, and what it guarded is left open. The human-move model would reach for it, and the engine would choose nothing else.
There is a deflection here, a defender drawn off the piece it protected. A natural move in the human-move model's eyes and a strong one in the engine's, though the engine has a favorite elsewhere.
The human-move model finds this natural, but it gives the other side a deflection. A defender could be lured away, leaving what it guards unprotected.
This lets the other side lure a defender off the piece it protects. The lone playable defense was a different move, and the human-move model rates it hard to spot.
Another move could have lured a defender away from its duty. This move is natural to the human-move model, and the defender keeps its watch.
